claims.claim: M-cell somatic responses to tectal stimulation decay to resting values 200–300 ms after the end of the tectal train.
claims.source: M-cell somatic responses reach a plateau after 30–100 ms and decay to resting values 200–300 ms after the end of the tectal train.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from the current study.

claims.claim: Increasing the duration of 60 Hz tectal trains drives stronger tectal responses due to the increase of the tonic component of the response.
claims.source: Increasing the duration of the 60 Hz trains drove stronger tectal responses due to the increase of the tonic component of the response while the phasic response remained unchanged (ANOVA, tonic: F(3,40) = 37.29, p < 0.0001, phasic: F(3,40) = 0.58, p = 0.6311, Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The phasic response to 60 Hz tectal trains remains unchanged when train duration is increased.
claims.source: Increasing the duration of the 60 Hz trains drove stronger tectal responses due to the increase of the tonic component of the response while the phasic response remained unchanged (ANOVA, tonic: F(3,40) = 37.29, p < 0.0001, phasic: F(3,40) = 0.58, p = 0.6311, Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Increasing the frequency of 100 ms tectal stimulation trains drives stronger tectal responses due to a large increase in the tonic component.
claims.source: Increasing the frequency of the 100 ms stimulation trains also drove stronger tectal responses due to a large increase in the tonic component (ANOVA, tonic: F(3,30) = 12.29, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Increasing the tectal stimulus frequency produces a significant reduction in the amplitude of the phasic component.
claims.source: However, increasing the tectal stimulus frequency produced a significant reduction in the amplitude of the phasic component (ANOVA, phasic: F(3,30) = 11.29, p < 0.0001, Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Increasing the duration of a 60 Hz train from 33 to 200 ms produces a 45% increase in the total response amplitude.
claims.source: Increasing the duration of a 60 Hz from 33 to 200 ms produced a 45% increase in the total response amplitude (phasic + tonic) while increasing the frequency from 30 to 200 Hz produced a 50% increase in the response amplitude (Figure 1B, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1D.

claims.claim: Increasing the frequency of a 100 ms train from 30 to 200 Hz produces a 50% increase in the response amplitude.
claims.source: Increasing the duration of a 60 Hz from 33 to 200 ms produced a 45% increase in the total response amplitude (phasic + tonic) while increasing the frequency from 30 to 200 Hz produced a 50% increase in the response amplitude (Figure 1B, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1D.

claims.claim: Multimodal integration depends on the strength of the unimodal components.
claims.source: Since multimodal integration is known to depend on the strength of the unimodal components (Stanford et al., 2005; Martorell and Medan, 2022), in the following multimodal experiments we leveraged this characterization to generate tectal stimuli of variable strength and dynamics.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on MSI principles.

claims.claim: If the perceived source localizations of two stimuli overlap, these stimuli are more likely to be integrated.
claims.source: If the perceived source localizations of two stimuli overlap, these stimuli are more likely to be integrated.
claims.evidence: This is a well-established principle of MSI supported by the cited references.

claims.claim: If two stimuli arrive from spatially disparate sources, the chances of observing MSI will decrease.
claims.source: Conversely, if the two stimuli arrive from spatially disparate sources the chances of observing an MSI will decrease (Meredith and Stein, 1996; Stein and Stanford, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a well-established principle of MSI supported by the cited references.

claims.claim: There are no statistical differences in M-cell responses between ipsi- and contralateral tectal stimulation.
claims.source: Analysis from pairs of tectal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, N = 9) and auditory (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, N = 11) M-cell responses showed no statistical differences between ipsi- and contralateral stimulation (paired T-test, T: t(8) = 0.18, p = 0.8573, A: t(10) = −0.76, p = 0.4672).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There are no statistical differences in M-cell responses between ipsi- and contralateral auditory stimulation.
claims.source: Analysis from pairs of tectal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, N = 9) and auditory (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, N = 11) M-cell responses showed no statistical differences between ipsi- and contralateral stimulation (paired T-test, T: t(8) = 0.18, p = 0.8573, A: t(10) = −0.76, p = 0.4672).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In goldfish, tectal stimulation produces responses with similar latency and amplitude in both M-cells.
claims.source: This confirms previous results indicating that in goldfish, tectal stimulation produces responses with similar latency and amplitude in both M-cells (Zottoli et al., 1987; Canfield, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and confirmed by current experimental data.

claims.claim: Abrupt sound stimuli have been extensively used to trigger the short latency escape responses initiated by firing of the M-cell.
claims.source: Abrupt sound stimuli have been extensively used to trigger the short latency escape responses initiated by firing of the M-cell (Eaton et al., 1977; Burgess and Granato, 2007; Neumeister et al., 2008; Weiss et al., 2009; Zheng and Schmid, 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Acoustic stimulation produces a complex response in the M-cell which is composed of a fast EPSP superimposed on a depolarizing envelope termed slow EPSP.
claims.source: Acoustic stimulation produces a complex response in the M-cell which is composed of a fast EPSP superimposed on a depolarizing envelope termed slow EPSP (Szabo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on M-cell auditory responses.

claims.claim: The fast EPSP in M-cell auditory responses is composed of fast electrical coupling potentials resulting from firing of the eighth nerve auditory afferences that synapse the distal end of the lateral dendrite of the M-cell (club endings).
claims.source: The fast EPSP is composed of fast electrical coupling potentials resulting from firing of the eighth nerve auditory afferences that synapse the distal end of the lateral dendrite of the M-cell (club endings) (Pereda et al., 2004; Szabo et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on M-cell synaptic physiology.

claims.claim: The slow EPSP in M-cell auditory responses is originated by chemical (glutamatergic) synaptic contacts on the soma and proximal dendrite conveying information from inner ear endorgans.
claims.source: In contrast, the slow EPSP is originated by chemical (glutamatergic) synaptic contacts on the soma and proximal dendrite conveying information from inner hear endorgans and it has been shown that it mostly carries information on stimulus intensity (Szabo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on M-cell synaptic physiology.

claims.claim: The slow EPSP mostly carries information on stimulus intensity.
claims.source: In contrast, the slow EPSP is originated by chemical (glutamatergic) synaptic contacts on the soma and proximal dendrite conveying information from inner hear endorgans and it has been shown that it mostly carries information on stimulus intensity (Szabo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on M-cell synaptic physiology.

claims.claim: Increasing the duration of 60 Hz tectal trains positively modulates multisensory responses in the M-cell.
claims.source: Increasing the duration of the 60 Hz tectal train positively modulated the multisensory responses (amplitudes ranging from 3.08 ± 0.84 to 5.29 ± 1.64 mV, N = 17, n = 47; LM: evoked depolarization ∼ tectal duration, F(1,45) = 17,39, p = 0.0001, Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Multisensory responses with 60 Hz tectal trains of varying duration show MSI/Max indices ranging from 1.48 to 1.53, indicating significant multisensory enhancement.
claims.source: When the multimodal responses were normalized to the most effective unisensory response, the resulting MSI/Max indices (see Methods), ranged from 1.48 to 1.53 across all stimulus durations (Wilcoxon single sample test mu = 1, alternative mu ≠ 1, p < 0.001 for all stimulus durations, Figure 2C), indicating a significant multisensory enhancement of the response.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Multisensory responses with 60 Hz tectal trains show MSI/Sum indices less than 1 (sublinear integration) for all cases except for the briefest tectal stimulus.
claims.source: When the multimodal response was normalized to the sum of both unisensory responses, the resulting MSI/Sum indices (see Methods) were less than 1 (i.e. sublinear integration, Wilcoxon single sample test mu = 1, alternative mu ≠ 1, p < 0.01) for all cases except for the briefest tectal stimulus, for which the MSI/Sum index was 1.06 (i.e. linear integration, Wilcoxon single sample test mu = 1, alternative mu ≠ 1, p < 0.0676, Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The briefest tectal stimulus (1 ms) combined with auditory stimulation shows linear integration (MSI/Sum index of 1.06).
claims.source: When the multimodal response was normalized to the sum of both unisensory responses, the resulting MSI/Sum indices (see Methods) were less than 1 (i.e. sublinear integration, Wilcoxon single sample test mu = 1, alternative mu ≠ 1, p < 0.01) for all cases except for the briefest tectal stimulus, for which the MSI/Sum index was 1.06 (i.e. linear integration, Wilcoxon single sample test mu = 1, alternative mu ≠ 1, p < 0.0676, Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Increasing the frequency of a 100-ms tectal train is not as effective in modulating multisensory responses as increasing train duration.
claims.source: Increasing the frequency of a 100-ms tectal train (Figure 2E) was not as effective in modulating the multisensory responses (LM: evoked depolarization ∼ tectal frequency, F(1,39) = 3.96, p = 0.0535, Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Multimodal responses with 100-ms tectal trains of varying frequency exhibit MSI/Max indices ranging 1.43–1.53.
claims.source: However, the multimodal responses still exhibited MSI/Max indices that ranged 1.43–1.53 when compared to the largest unimodal stimulus (Figure 2G) indicating that a 100-ms tectal train (irrespective of its frequency) significantly enhances the M-cell response.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: A 100-ms tectal train (irrespective of its frequency) significantly enhances the M-cell response when combined with auditory stimulation.
claims.source: However, the multimodal responses still exhibited MSI/Max indices that ranged 1.43–1.53 when compared to the largest unimodal stimulus (Figure 2G) indicating that a 100-ms tectal train (irrespective of its frequency) significantly enhances the M-cell response.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The MSI/Sum of multimodal responses with 100-ms tectal trains ranges 0.82–0.86, showing sublinear integration.
claims.source: The MSI/Sum of these multimodal responses ranged 0.82–0.86 showing a similar sublinear integration to that of the multisensory stimuli with the longer 60 Hz trains (Wilcoxon single sample test mu = 1, alternative mu ≠ 1, all p ≤ 0.01, Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Neither MSI/Max nor MSI/Sum shows a significant dependency with tectal frequency.
claims.source: Neither MSI/Max nor MSI/Sum showed a significant dependency with tectal frequency (LM: MSI/Max ∼ tectal frequency, F(1,39) = 0.02, p = 0.882, MSI/Sum ∼ tectal frequency, F(1,39) = 0.49, p = 0.487).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Combining an auditory pip with a preceding tectal pulse enhances the M-cell response by about 50% in all cases.
claims.source: Overall, these results show that, in all cases, combining an auditory pip with a preceding tectal pulse enhances the M-cell response by about 50%.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data across multiple conditions.

claims.claim: Multisensory enhancement in the M-cell does not show a strong modulation by the duration or frequency of the tectal stimulus.
claims.source: This multisensory enhancement does not show a strong modulation by the duration or frequency of the tectal stimulus (Figure 2C, G).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2G.

claims.claim: Most multisensory stimuli exhibit sublinear integration in the M-cell.
claims.source: However, while most multisensory stimuli exhibited a sublinear integration, the multisensory stimulus with the shortest (and weakest) tectal component produced a linear response (Figure 2B, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claims.claim: The multisensory stimulus with the shortest (and weakest) tectal component produces a linear response in the M-cell.
claims.source: However, while most multisensory stimuli exhibited a sublinear integration, the multisensory stimulus with the shortest (and weakest) tectal component produced a linear response (Figure 2B, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claims.claim: Both visual and auditory stimuli evoke FFI at the perisomatic region of the M-cell through a population of inhibitory interneurons.
claims.source: Both visual and auditory stimuli evoke FFI at the perisomatic region of the M-cell through a population of inhibitory interneurons which open chloride channels that produce shunting of the postsynaptic currents (Diamond et al., 1973; Zottoli et al., 1987; Koyama et al., 2011; Tabor et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on M-cell inhibition.

claims.claim: FFI restricts the temporal window of sensory excitation to terminate the excitatory signal in the M-cell.
claims.source: This FFI restricts the temporal window of sensory excitation to terminate the excitatory signal.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of FFI in neural circuits.

claims.claim: Peak FFI inhibition induced by auditory and tectal stimulation shows similar amplitude.
claims.source: Peak FFI inhibition induced by auditory and tectal stimulation showed similar amplitude (Figure 3B, auditory vs. tectal %SI: 13.65 ± 4.74 vs. 14.55 ± 7.50; Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared (1) = 0.01, p = 0.9066, N = 19) with peak inhibition at the same time (auditory vs. tectal time (ms) of maximum %SI: 9.04 ± 3.93 vs. 8.85 ± 6.54; Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared (1) = 0.30, p = 0.5838, Figure 3C, N = 19).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Peak inhibition from auditory and tectal FFI occurs at the same time.
claims.source: Peak FFI inhibition induced by auditory and tectal stimulation showed similar amplitude (Figure 3B, auditory vs. tectal %SI: 13.65 ± 4.74 vs. 14.55 ± 7.50; Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared (1) = 0.01, p = 0.9066, N = 19) with peak inhibition at the same time (auditory vs. tectal time (ms) of maximum %SI: 9.04 ± 3.93 vs. 8.85 ± 6.54; Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared (1) = 0.30, p = 0.5838, Figure 3C, N = 19).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Recovery from inhibition is much faster for tectal than for auditory FFI.
claims.source: Although the maximum level of inhibition was comparable and was reached in a similar time, recovery from inhibition was much faster for tectal than for auditory FFI.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: Tectal FFI decays to 50% of its peak in 8 ms.
claims.source: Tectal FFI decayed to 50% of its peak in 8 ms, compared to 30 ms for the auditory FFI (Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared (1) = 5.97, p = 0.0145, Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Auditory FFI decays to 50% of its peak in 30 ms.
claims.source: Tectal FFI decayed to 50% of its peak in 8 ms, compared to 30 ms for the auditory FFI (Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared (1) = 5.97, p = 0.0145, Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The area under the curve for auditory FFI is almost three times greater than for tectal FFI.
claims.source: In addition, the area under the curve for auditory FFI was almost three times greater than for tectal FFI (502 vs. 176%*ms, respectively, Kruskal–Wallis chi-squared (1) = 5.58, p = 0.0181, Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Auditory stimuli trigger more prolonged inhibition than tectal stimuli of similar amplitude and decay time.
claims.source: These results highlight the key role of the temporal dynamics of the inhibition that reaches the M-cell and which in turn will affect integration in the M-cell. Moreover, these results show that auditory stimuli trigger more prolonged inhibition than tectal stimuli of similar amplitude and decay time.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The short-lived FFI that follows tectal stimulation suggests that multiple trains or waves of tectal inputs are more likely to be integrated and summed than multiple sounds.
claims.source: The short-lived FFI that follows tectal stimulation suggests that multiple trains or waves of tectal inputs are more likely to be integrated and summed than multiple sounds.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in FFI decay dynamics.

claims.claim: Auditory inputs from the eighth nerve reach the distal lateral dendrite of the M-cell through a disynaptic (≈2 ms) pathway.
claims.source: First, auditory inputs from the eighth nerve reach the distal lateral dendrite of the M-cell through a disynaptic (≈2 ms) pathway followed by slower inputs from glutamatergic synaptic contacts on the soma and proximal dendrite.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by prior anatomical and physiological studies cited earlier in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Visual inputs reach the ventral dendrite after a polysynaptic (≈20 ms) pathway that includes the optic tectum.
claims.source: Visual inputs reach the ventral dendrite after a polysynaptic (≈20 ms) pathway that includes the optic tectum (Zottoli et al., 1987; Szabo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical and physiological studies.

claims.claim: M-cell dendritic characteristics determine modality specific filtering differences resulting in stronger attenuation of visual than auditory signals.
claims.source: Second, M-cell dendritic characteristics determine modality specific filtering differences resulting in stronger attenuation of visual than auditory signals (Medan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on M-cell dendritic properties.

claims.claim: A sound pip that precedes by 20–150 ms a second sound reduces the M-cell response to the second sound, a phenomenon known as auditory prepulse inhibition.
claims.source: For auditory stimuli, it has been reported that a sound pip that precedes by 20–150 ms a second sound reduces the M-cell response to the second sound, a phenomenon known as auditory prepulse inhibition (Neumeister et al., 2008; Curtin and Preuss, 2015; Tabor et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on auditory prepulse inhibition.

claims.claim: The mean lingering depolarization remaining 50 ms after stimulus onset is slightly larger for auditory pips than for tectal stimuli.
claims.source: The mean lingering depolarization remaining immediately before the second stimulus was delivered (Figure 4A, top trace, pink bar) was slightly larger for the evoked auditory pip than for the tectal stimulus (Figure 4B, A: 1.48 ± 0.79 mV vs. T: 0.95 ± 0.50 mV, Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test (1) = 5.5173, p = 0.0188).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In AA trials (auditory-auditory), the first auditory pip reduces the amplitude expected for the second pip by 42%, showing inhibitory integration.
claims.source: In the AA trials (N = 21), we observed an inhibitory integration (S1–S2 Int./Sum < 1, two-sided Wilcoxon rank test, p < 0.0001) with the first auditory pip reducing the amplitude expected for the second pip by 42%, as others have previously described (Neumeister et al., 2008; Curtin and Preuss, 2015; Tabor et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The AT combination (auditory-tectal) shows sublinear integration.
claims.source: The AT combination also showed sublinear integration (S1–S2 Int./Sum < 1, two-sided Wilcoxon rank test, p = 0.0078) while the TT and TA combinations showed linear integration (S1–S2 Int./Sum = 1, two-sided Wilcoxon rank test, VA: p = 0.0681, VV: p = 0.9453, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The TT combination (tectal-tectal) shows linear integration.
claims.source: The AT combination also showed sublinear integration (S1–S2 Int./Sum < 1, two-sided Wilcoxon rank test, p = 0.0078) while the TT and TA combinations showed linear integration (S1–S2 Int./Sum = 1, two-sided Wilcoxon rank test, VA: p = 0.0681, VV: p = 0.9453, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The TA combination (tectal-auditory) shows linear integration.
claims.source: The AT combination also showed sublinear integration (S1–S2 Int./Sum < 1, two-sided Wilcoxon rank test, p = 0.0078) while the TT and TA combinations showed linear integration (S1–S2 Int./Sum = 1, two-sided Wilcoxon rank test, VA: p = 0.0681, VV: p = 0.9453, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect in the AA combination is significantly larger than for the AT combination.
claims.source: The inhibitory effect in the AA combination was significantly larger than for the AT combination (Figure 4, 1w-ANOVA, F = 38.34, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: There is a significant inverse correlation between the magnitude of multisensory enhancement and the magnitude of the unisensory components.
claims.source: We found a significant inverse correlation between the magnitude of the multisensory enhancement and the magnitude of the unisensory components (MSI/Max, LM, F(1,172): 28.17, p < 0.0001; MSI/Sum, LM, F(1,172): 67.33, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of pooled experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The inverse effectiveness observed at the M-cell level parallels the inverse effectiveness reported at the behavioral level in goldfish.
claims.source: This result parallels the inverse effectiveness reported at the behavioral level in goldfish (McIntyre and Preuss, 2019; Martorell and Medan, 2022), confirming that the relative multisensory enhancement obtained by combining two inputs is proportionally higher when the stimuli are weak.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of current experimental data with prior behavioral studies.

claims.claim: Combinations of weak stimuli (<2.5 mV) produce supralinear multisensory responses that are between 50–100% stronger than the most effective unisensory stimulus.
claims.source: Combinations of weak stimuli (<2.5 mV, Figure 5B) produce supralinear multisensory responses that are between 50–100% stronger than the most effective unisensory stimulus (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: Inverse effectiveness of MSI is implemented at the single (Mauthner) cell level in the escape network of fish.
claims.source: Noteworthy, these results provide robust evidence that in the escape network of fish, inverse effectiveness of MSI is implemented, at least, at the single (Mauthner) cell level.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The M-cell incorporates multisensory information to enhance its responses.
claims.source: Here, we show that the M-cell incorporates multisensory information to enhance its responses and characterize how the integration of multiple stimuli is affected by the modality, spatial source, temporal structure, temporal order, and intensity of the stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claims.claim: MSI in the M-cell has an unequivocal function in fish behavior and survival, as it directly determines whether and when a C-start is triggered.
claims.source: In contrast to other known multisensory structures of vertebrates MSI in the M-cell has an unequivocal function in fish behavior and survival, as it directly determines whether and when a C-start is triggered (McIntyre and Preuss, 2019; Martorell and Medan, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the known one-to-one relationship between M-cell firing and C-start initiation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Sensory inputs are subject to different passive decays depending on the site of the dendritic arbor at which they arrive in the M-cell.
claims.source: First, sensory inputs are subject to different passive decays depending on the site of the dendritic arbor at which they arrive.
claims.evidence: This is based on known biophysical properties of dendritic signal propagation.

claims.claim: Auditory inputs reach the M-cell distal lateral dendrite through dense mixed electrical and chemical synapses driven through the posterior eighth nerve afferents.
claims.source: Auditory inputs reach the M-cell distal lateral dendrite through dense mixed electrical and chemical synapses driven through the posterior eighth nerve afferents and the proximal dendrite through indirect glutamatergic inputs conveying information from inner ear endorgans (Szabo et al., 2006; Szabo et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical and physiological studies.

claims.claim: Visual inputs arriving to the ventral dendrite establish synapses that do not show additional specializations as the club endings.
claims.source: In contrast, visual inputs arriving to the ventral dendrite establish synapses that do not show additional specializations as the club endings (Zottoli et al., 1987; Cachope et al., 2007; Szabo et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claims.claim: The geometrical properties of the M-cell lateral and ventral dendrites (length and tapering) impose different filters on the input signal.
claims.source: Second, the geometrical properties of the M-cell lateral and ventral dendrites (length and tapering) impose different filters on the input signal which determine a stronger spatial decay for visual than for auditory signals (Medan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on M-cell dendritic properties.

claims.claim: Active ion conductances decrease the membrane resistance and impact the response to following signals as excitatory (and inhibitory) signals reach the soma.
claims.source: Third, as excitatory (and inhibitory) signals reach the soma, the active ion conductances decrease the membrane resistance and impact the response to following signals (Hodgkin, 1947).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on fundamental biophysical principles supported by a classic citation.

claims.claim: Abrupt auditory pips generate fast EPSPs that depend on the stimulus frequency and a depolarizing envelope proportional to the stimulus amplitude.
claims.source: Both abrupt auditory pips and longer lasting auditory looms generate fast EPSPs that depend on the stimulus frequency and a depolarizing envelope proportional to the stimulus amplitude (Szabo et al., 2006) that slowly decays to baseline (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to experimental data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Tectal responses consist of fast peaks that track stimulus frequency and a tonic depolarizing envelope proportional both to stimulus duration and frequency.
claims.source: Although the pathways for auditory and visual inputs are completely different, tectal responses also consist of fast peaks that track stimulus frequency and a tonic depolarizing envelope proportional both to stimulus duration and frequency (Figure 1) that also decays slowly (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claims.claim: The temporal dynamics of the responses modulate the effective MSI in the M-cell soma.
claims.source: These temporal dynamics of the responses modulate the effective MSI in the M-cell soma, which emerges as a complex, nonlinear interaction between 'positive' (input strength and summation, voltage-dependent depolarizing conductances) and 'negative' (temporal and spatial decay, FFI, and depolarization-induced decrease in input resistance) contributions.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental findings and known biophysical mechanisms.

claims.claim: Fish exhibit a behavioral multisensory enhancement of the C-start escape response for audiovisual stimuli.
claims.source: We have previously shown that fish exhibit a behavioral multisensory enhancement of the C-start escape response for audiovisual stimuli, and that this effect is reduced when increasing the salience of the unisensory stimuli (Martorell and Medan, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior behavioral research.

claims.claim: The behavioral multisensory enhancement effect is reduced when increasing the salience of the unisensory stimuli.
claims.source: We have previously shown that fish exhibit a behavioral multisensory enhancement of the C-start escape response for audiovisual stimuli, and that this effect is reduced when increasing the salience of the unisensory stimuli (Martorell and Medan, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior behavioral research.

claims.claim: The response evoked by an auditory pip can be increased by about 50% when it is preceded by a tectal stimulus.
claims.source: Paralleling our previous behavioral results, here we show through intracellular recordings that the response evoked by an auditory pip can be increased by about 50% when it is preceded by a tectal stimulus (Figure 2C, G).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2G.

claims.claim: The multisensory enhancement in the M-cell was not affected by relatively large changes in stimulus frequency.
claims.source: This enhancement was not affected by relatively large changes in stimulus frequency.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data across different stimulus frequencies.

claims.claim: The plateau in the tonic depolarization observed 30–50 ms after a sustained stimulus combined with the low-pass filtering properties of the membrane could be responsible for the lack of frequency effects.
claims.source: The plateau in the tonic depolarization observed 30–50 ms after a sustained stimulus (Figure 1A) combined with the low-pass filtering properties of the membrane could be responsible for the lack of frequency effects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on observed data and known membrane properties.

claims.claim: The M-cell functions as a 'sudden' stimulus detector rather than a precise coder of sensory stimulus properties.
claims.source: These two mechanisms point to the M-cell role as a 'sudden' stimulus detector rather than a precise coder of sensory stimulus properties.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed response properties of the M-cell.

claims.claim: Cellular biophysics predict a sublinear integration of subthreshold inputs due to a reduction in the driving force of sodium and the aperture of ion channels that reduce the membrane resistance.
claims.source: This sublinear effect was expected in the case of passive integration, since cellular biophysics predict a sublinear integration of subthreshold inputs due to a reduction in the driving force of sodium and the aperture of ion channels that reduce the membrane resistance.
claims.evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles of neuronal integration.

claims.claim: Auditory stimuli evoked firing in 5% of M-cells tested.
claims.source: Indeed, analysis of 60 M-cells tested with A, tectal and multimodal stimuli showed that auditory stimuli evoked firing in 5% of cells, tectal stimuli in 6.7% of cells but almost 12% of M-cells fired in response to multisensory stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data from 60 M-cells.

claims.claim: Tectal stimuli evoked firing in 6.7% of M-cells tested.
claims.source: Indeed, analysis of 60 M-cells tested with A, tectal and multimodal stimuli showed that auditory stimuli evoked firing in 5% of cells, tectal stimuli in 6.7% of cells but almost 12% of M-cells fired in response to multisensory stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data from 60 M-cells.

claims.claim: Almost 12% of M-cells fired in response to multisensory stimuli.
claims.source: Indeed, analysis of 60 M-cells tested with A, tectal and multimodal stimuli showed that auditory stimuli evoked firing in 5% of cells, tectal stimuli in 6.7% of cells but almost 12% of M-cells fired in response to multisensory stimuli.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data from 60 M-cells.

claims.claim: The firing probabilities reported are probably an underestimation of actual firing probabilities due to anesthesia and paralyzing agents.
claims.source: Even though these results are probably an underestimation of actual firing probabilities due to anesthesia and paralyzing agents, they provide a mechanistic support to our previous behavioral observations (Martorell and Medan, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known effects of anesthesia on neural excitability.

claims.claim: There exists one or more active mechanism/s of MSI upstream of the M-cell soma or locally at the level of the dendritic tree of the M-cell.
claims.source: This suggests the existence of one or more active mechanism/s of MSI upstream of the M-cell soma, potentially through a presynaptic neuron that also receives audiovisual inputs and projects to the M-cell or locally at the level of the dendritic tree of the M-cell.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed linear integration of weak stimuli.

claims.claim: The M-cell membrane has nonlinearities in the lateral and ventral dendrites which progressively increase M-cell excitability for depolarizations above 5 mV.
claims.source: Moreover, previous work has described the M-cell membrane nonlinearities in the lateral and ventral dendrites which progressively increase M-cell excitability for depolarizations above 5 mV (Faber and Korn, 1986; Medan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on M-cell membrane properties.

claims.claim: Nonlinear membrane properties might enhance MSI of weak stimuli, providing a cellular mechanism for the principle of inverse effectiveness of MSI.
claims.source: Such nonlinear properties might enhance MSI of weak stimuli (Martorell and Medan, 2022) providing a cellular mechanism for the principle of inverse effectiveness of MSI.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting membrane properties to MSI principles.

claims.claim: The lengthy decay of the slow EPSP of the auditory pip (or the tonic component of the tectal train) probably contributed to relax the requirement for coincident inputs, effectively broadening the temporal window of integration.
claims.source: As it has been previously suggested, the lengthy decay of the slow EPSP of the auditory pip (or the tonic component of the tectal train) probably contributed to relax the requirement for coincident inputs, effectively broadening the temporal window of integration (Szabo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed temporal dynamics and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The difference in integration between AA and AT stimuli might be due to differences in both the presynaptic networks that mediate PPI and in the temporal decay of auditory and tectally evoked FFI.
claims.source: This difference might be due to differences in both the presynaptic networks that mediate PPI (Tabor et al., 2018) and in the temporal decay of auditory and tectally evoked FFI (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and prior research.

claims.claim: If auditory stimulation recruits inhibitory PHP neurons that target the proximal lateral dendrite of the M-cell, a subsequent sensory input propagating along the lateral dendrite would suffer stronger attenuation than one reaching the soma through the ventral dendrite.
claims.source: If auditory stimulation recruits inhibitory PHP neurons that target the proximal lateral dendrite of the M-cell, a subsequent sensory input propagating along the lateral dendrite (i.e, auditory input) would suffer stronger attenuation than one reaching the soma through the ventral dendrite (i.e. tectal input).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the spatial distribution of inhibition.

claims.claim: A subset of glutamatergic Gsx1 neurons located in rhombomere 4 mediate M-cell auditory presynaptic inhibition.
claims.source: A subset of glutamatergic Gsx1 neurons located in rhombomere 4 have been shown to mediate M-cell auditory presynaptic inhibition (Tabor et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Gsx1 neurons produce presynaptic inhibition of eighth nerve auditory fibers adjacent to the distal portion of the M-cell lateral dendrite but leave unaffected the ventral dendrite.
claims.source: These neurons produce presynaptic inhibition of eighth nerve auditory fibers adjacent to the distal portion of the M-cell lateral dendrite but leave unaffected the ventral dendrite.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on prior research on presynaptic inhibition mechanisms.

claims.claim: The presynaptic inhibition mechanism could affect the processing of pairs of sensory signals that initiate with an auditory component (AA, AT) and leave the integration of tectal or multisensory stimuli unaffected.
claims.source: This mechanism could therefore affect the processing of pairs of sensory signals that initiate with an auditory component (AA, AT) and leave the integration of tectal or multisensory stimuli unaffected.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of presynaptic inhibition.

claims.claim: Adult goldfish (Carassius auratus) of both sexes and 7–10 cm of standard body length were used in the study.
claims.source: We used adult goldfish (Carassius auratus) of both sexes and 7–10 cm of standard body length.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental subjects.

claims.source: Sound stimuli consisted in single-cycle sound pips (5 ms duration at 200 Hz) produced by a function generator (33210A Agilent Technologies Inc, Santa Clara, CA, USA) connected to a shielded subwoofer (SA-WN250 Sony Corp., Tokyo, Japan) located 30 cm to the right from the recording chamber.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental stimuli.

claims.source: For all experiments we used a sound intensity of 118 dB SPL (relative to 1 μPa in water), except for the experiments in Figure 4 where we used a sound intensity of 147 dB SPL (relative to 1 μPa in water).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental parameters.

claims.claim: Only 3 out of 60 M-cells (5%) fired at least once to an auditory stimulus.
claims.source: Post hoc analysis of the M-cell responses in this study revealed that only 3 out of 60 M-cells (5%) fired at least once to an auditory stimulus.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from post hoc analysis of experimental data.

results.result: M-cell responses to tectal stimulation are modulated by stimulus duration and frequency. Increasing the duration of 60 Hz trains increases the tonic component while the phasic component remains unchanged. Increasing the frequency of 100 ms trains increases the tonic component but decreases the phasic component. Both manipulations produce approximately 45-50% increases in total response amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 are well-supported by statistical analyses (ANOVA) with significant p-values and clear presentation of data in Figure 1. The experimental design appropriately separates tonic and phasic components, and the quantitative results are consistent across different stimulus parameters.

results.result: Combining auditory and tectal stimuli produces multisensory enhancement in the M-cell of approximately 50% (MSI/Max ~1.5). Most stimulus combinations show sublinear integration (MSI/Sum < 1), except for the briefest tectal stimulus which shows linear integration. The enhancement is relatively insensitive to tectal stimulus duration or frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C60 are supported by appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon tests, linear models) with significant p-values and data shown in Figure 2. The MSI/Max and MSI/Sum metrics are properly defined and applied. The finding of linear integration for weak stimuli versus sublinear for stronger stimuli is particularly well-documented.

results.result: Auditory and tectal stimuli evoke feedforward inhibition (FFI) with similar peak amplitude and timing, but auditory FFI decays much more slowly than tectal FFI. Tectal FFI decays to 50% in 8 ms versus 30 ms for auditory FFI, and the area under the curve for auditory FFI is approximately three times greater.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C69 are well-supported by statistical analyses (Kruskal-Wallis tests) with significant p-values and clear presentation in Figure 3. The experimental design using antidromic action potentials to measure shunting inhibition is appropriate. The differential decay dynamics are quantitatively characterized and provide mechanistic insight into MSI.

results.result: Stimulus temporal order and modality affect integration in the M-cell. Auditory-auditory (AA) pairs show strong inhibitory integration (42% reduction), while auditory-tectal (AT) shows weaker sublinear integration, and tectal-tectal (TT) and tectal-auditory (TA) show linear integration when stimuli are separated by 50 ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 are supported by appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon rank tests, ANOVA) with significant p-values and data shown in Figure 4. The experimental design systematically varies stimulus order and modality. The differential integration patterns are consistent with the FFI decay dynamics reported in Figure 3.

results.result: Multisensory integration in the M-cell exhibits inverse effectiveness: the magnitude of multisensory enhancement is inversely correlated with the strength of unisensory components. Weak stimuli (<2.5 mV) produce supralinear responses 50-100% stronger than the most effective unisensory stimulus, demonstrating that inverse effectiveness is implemented at the single-cell level.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are well-supported by linear model analyses with highly significant p-values (p < 0.0001) and clear presentation in Figure 5. The pooling of data across multiple experimental conditions (N=18, n=174) provides robust evidence. The parallel between cellular and behavioral inverse effectiveness strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Tectal stimulation at 30 s ITI produces non-adapting M-cell responses that are qualitatively and quantitatively similar to visual looming stimuli, though tectal stimulation likely recruits projections that are predominantly but not exclusively visual.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C28 are supported by experimental observations and citations to prior work. The methodological choice to use tectal stimulation is justified by the need to avoid adaptation. The caveat about multisensory tectum inputs (C25-C26) is appropriately acknowledged, though this introduces some uncertainty about the purely visual nature of the stimulus.

results.result: M-cell responses to tectal and auditory stimulation show no statistical differences between ipsilateral and contralateral stimulation, confirming that both M-cells respond similarly to stimuli from either side.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are supported by paired t-tests with non-significant p-values and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. This control experiment validates pooling data from left and right M-cells and addresses potential spatial coherence concerns for MSI.

results.result: Multisensory stimuli evoke M-cell firing more frequently (12%) than auditory (5%) or tectal (6.7%) stimuli alone, though these probabilities likely underestimate actual firing rates due to anesthesia and paralysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 are based on analysis of 60 M-cells and provide quantitative support for multisensory enhancement at the level of action potential generation. The caveat about anesthesia effects (C105) is appropriately noted. However, no statistical test is provided to determine if the difference between 12% and 5-6.7% is significant.

results.result: M-cell somatic responses to tectal stimulation reach a plateau after 30-100 ms and decay to resting values 200-300 ms after the end of the tectal train.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 describe temporal dynamics of M-cell responses based on experimental observations. These are descriptive findings that characterize the time course of responses and are supported by the data shown in the figures.

results.result: The temporal dynamics of M-cell responses modulate MSI through complex nonlinear interactions between positive factors (input summation, voltage-dependent conductances) and negative factors (decay, FFI, decreased input resistance). The plateau in tonic depolarization and low-pass filtering may explain the lack of frequency effects, suggesting the M-cell functions as a sudden stimulus detector.
results.evaluation: Claims C94, C99-C100 represent interpretive synthesis of the experimental findings. These inferences are reasonable given the data presented, though they involve some speculation about mechanisms. The characterization of the M-cell as a sudden stimulus detector is consistent with the observed response properties.

results.result: Linear integration of weak multisensory stimuli suggests the existence of active MSI mechanisms upstream of the M-cell soma or in the dendritic tree. Nonlinear membrane properties that increase excitability above 5 mV might provide a cellular mechanism for inverse effectiveness.
results.evaluation: Claims C106 and C108 are speculative inferences about mechanisms that could explain the observed linear integration of weak stimuli. While C107 cites prior work on membrane nonlinearities, the connection to MSI inverse effectiveness remains hypothetical. These claims identify important questions for future work but lack direct experimental support in the current study.

results.result: Differences in integration between AA and AT stimuli may result from differences in presynaptic networks mediating prepulse inhibition and differential FFI decay dynamics. Spatial distribution of inhibition targeting different dendritic regions could contribute to modality-specific integration patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111, C114 propose mechanistic explanations for observed integration differences but are largely speculative. While C110 references experimental data (Figure 3D) and prior work, C111 explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about spatial distribution of inhibition. These represent reasonable hypotheses requiring additional experimental validation.

results.result: Background claims establishing that MSI combines information from multiple modalities to create coherent perception, is widespread across species, enhances escape behaviors, and exhibits inverse effectiveness with stimulus strength.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C16 represent established knowledge in the field supported by multiple citations. These provide appropriate context for the current study and are well-documented in the literature.

results.result: Anatomical and physiological background on M-cell circuitry: auditory inputs reach the lateral dendrite via a fast disynaptic pathway while visual inputs reach the ventral dendrite via a slower polysynaptic pathway through the tectum. The dendrites have different cable properties suited to processing different stimulus types.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21, C71-C73, C88-C90 describe established anatomical and physiological properties of the M-cell system, supported by multiple citations to prior work. These provide essential background for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Additional background claims on goldfish adaptation to looming stimuli, tectal multisensory integration, MSI principles, M-cell synaptic physiology, FFI mechanisms, prepulse inhibition, behavioral MSI effects, and biophysical properties of neuronal integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C25, C37-C39, C43-C47, C61-C62, C74, C86-C87, C91-C93, C95-C96, C101, C107, C109, C112-C113 represent established knowledge supported by citations or fundamental biophysical principles. These provide necessary context and mechanistic framework for the study.

results.result: Summary claims that stimulus modality, intensity, temporal structure, and interstimulus delay affect input summation in the M-cell, and that distinct FFI decay dynamics account for certain aspects of integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C8, C85 are high-level summary statements of the main findings, supported by the detailed experimental results in other claim groups. These accurately represent the scope and conclusions of the study.

results.result: Methodological details: adult goldfish (7-10 cm) were used; sound stimuli were 5 ms, 200 Hz pips at 118 dB SPL (147 dB for Figure 4 experiments); only 5% of M-cells fired to auditory stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 are straightforward methodological statements supported by the Methods section and post-hoc analysis. These provide important details for reproducibility and interpretation.

results.result: Intracellular recordings show that auditory responses can be increased by about 50% when preceded by tectal stimulation, and this enhancement is not affected by large changes in stimulus frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 summarize key findings from the multisensory experiments, supported by data in Figures 2C and 2G. These parallel the behavioral observations and represent important cellular-level confirmation of MSI.

results.result: The short-lived tectal FFI suggests that multiple tectal inputs are more likely to be integrated than multiple auditory inputs.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 is a reasonable inference based on the differential FFI decay dynamics shown in Figure 3. This prediction is consistent with the known duration of effective visual looming stimuli, though direct experimental validation would strengthen the claim.

results.result: The authors characterize how tectal stimulation parameters (duration and frequency) affect M-cell responses. Increasing train duration increases the tonic component while the phasic component remains unchanged. Increasing frequency increases the tonic component but reduces the phasic component. Overall, both manipulations produce 45-50% increases in total response amplitude.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe this as 'necessary groundwork in calibrating tectal stimulation for maximal M-cell MSI' and note the results are 'convincing and well-supported.' The experimental approaches and stimulus parameter selection are described as 'clear and informed by the bibliography.'

results.result: Combining auditory pips with preceding tectal stimulation enhances M-cell responses by approximately 50% across various tectal stimulus durations and frequencies. Most combinations show sublinear integration (MSI/Sum < 1), except the briefest tectal stimulus which shows linear integration. The multisensory enhancement does not show strong modulation by tectal stimulus duration or frequency.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state the authors 'characterize this MSI with slightly varying tectal and acoustic inputs' and describe the empirical results as 'convincing and well-supported.' One reviewer notes the finding is 'nice, but unsurprising' that stimulus strength affects MSI similarly for M-cell physiology as previously shown for behavior.

results.result: Auditory and tectal stimuli evoke feedforward inhibition (FFI) with similar peak amplitude and timing, but recovery from inhibition is much faster for tectal FFI (8 ms to 50% decay) than auditory FFI (30 ms). The area under the curve for auditory FFI is almost three times greater than tectal FFI. These distinct decay dynamics can account for certain aspects of input integration in the M-cell.
results.evaluation: Reviewers identify this as 'the most compelling new observation' and state these are 'novel results that would be of interest to a broader sensory neuroscience community.' They describe the quantification of FFI from two sources and 'the logical extension of these FFI dynamics to M-cell physiology during MSI' as particularly valuable.

results.result: When pairs of stimuli are separated by 50 ms, auditory-auditory (AA) combinations show strong inhibitory integration (42% reduction), auditory-tectal (AT) shows sublinear integration, while tectal-tectal (TT) and tectal-auditory (TA) combinations show linear integration. The inhibitory effect in AA is significantly larger than in AT.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the authors 'assess the ability of the first stimulus to suppress responses to the second' and describe the findings as part of the convincing empirical results. The experimental approaches are described as 'well-informed electrophysiological approaches.'

results.result: There is a significant inverse correlation between multisensory enhancement magnitude and unisensory component strength. Weak stimuli (<2.5 mV) produce supralinear responses 50-100% stronger than the most effective unisensory stimulus. This inverse effectiveness at the M-cell level parallels behavioral observations in goldfish and provides evidence that inverse effectiveness is implemented at the single cell level.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note 'it is also nice, but unsurprising, to see that the relationship between stimulus strength that MSI is similar for M-cell physiology to what has previously been shown for behavior.' They describe the manuscript as showing 'M-cell physiology mirrors previously reported behavioural data in which stronger stimuli underwent less integration.'

results.result: Analysis of 60 M-cells shows that auditory stimuli evoked firing in 5% of cells, tectal stimuli in 6.7%, but multisensory stimuli evoked firing in almost 12% of M-cells. These firing probabilities are likely underestimations due to anesthesia and paralyzing agents.
results.evaluation: While reviewers state 'supporting evidence is generally convincing,' they specifically note that 'material reporting the direct control of behavior is less representative of the data.' This suggests some concern about the behavioral relevance claims, though the physiological data itself appears accepted.

results.result: The M-cell incorporates multisensory information to enhance its responses, and this MSI has an unequivocal function in fish behavior and survival as it directly determines whether and when a C-start is triggered.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the study 'provides valuable advances in our understanding of how inputs from multiple sources can impact the physiology of motor neurons during the process of multisensory integration' and note the major finding is that 'multisensory integration increases the certainty of environmental information in an inherently noisy environment.'

results.result: Tectal stimulation at 30 s ITI does not produce adaptation and results in depolarization responses similar to visual looming stimuli. Tectal stimulation likely recruits predominantly but not exclusively visual projections, reaching the distal ventral dendrite and producing non-adapting synaptic responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the experimental approaches as 'clear and informed by the bibliography' and note the authors 'performed well-informed electrophysiological approaches.' The methodological choices are implicitly accepted through the overall positive assessment of the study.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C31-C36 regarding tectal stimulation calibration and M-cell response characterization. Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers describing it as 'necessary groundwork' and 'convincing and well-supported,' matching OpenEval's assessment of appropriate statistical analyses and experimental design.

Complete agreement on claims C48-C60 regarding MSI characterization with varying stimulus parameters. Both find evidence SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note findings are 'convincing and well-supported' though 'nice, but unsurprising,' while OpenEval emphasizes the well-documented linear vs. sublinear integration patterns.

Strong agreement on claims C63-C69 regarding FFI decay dynamics, both finding evidence SUPPORTED. Peer review includes additional claims C70 and C8, describing this as 'the most compelling new observation' and 'novel results,' while OpenEval focuses on the statistical rigor and mechanistic insights. Both recognize the significance of differential decay dynamics.

Perfect agreement on claims C75-C80 regarding stimulus order effects and suppression. Both evaluations find evidence SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers noting 'well-informed electrophysiological approaches' and OpenEval highlighting consistency with FFI decay dynamics from Figure 3.

Complete agreement on claims C81-C84 regarding cellular-behavioral parallels in inverse effectiveness. Both find evidence SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers note it is 'nice, but unsurprising' that M-cell physiology mirrors behavioral data, while OpenEval emphasizes the robust statistical evidence from pooled data.

Agreement on claims C23-C28 regarding methodological choices for tectal stimulation. Both find evidence SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers describing approaches as 'clear and informed by the bibliography,' while OpenEval notes appropriate justification with some uncertainty about purely visual stimulus nature.

Disagreement on claims C102-C105 regarding behavioral relevance and action potential generation. OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED but notes lack of statistical testing for enhancement differences. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, specifically noting 'material reporting the direct control of behavior is less representative of the data.'

Both address high-level summary claims including C85. OpenEval (R16) covers C4-C8, C85 as main findings summary, while peer review (R7) addresses C85-C86 regarding broader understanding of multisensory integration. Both find evidence SUPPORTED and recognize the study's contribution to understanding MSI.

OpenEval R19 addresses claim C70 specifically as a prediction about visual looming stimulus duration, finding it SUPPORTED as reasonable inference. Peer R3 includes C70 among the 'most compelling new observations' about FFI dynamics, also finding it SUPPORTED but within broader context of C63-C69.
